blocks.html:
In order to promote international cooperation, USI has concluded MoU and educational agreements with numerous universities and other institutions around the world.

The different types of agreements are listed and described below:

  1. Memorandum of Understanding (MoU)
  2. Double Degree Agreement
  3. Joint Degree Agreement
  4. Accelerated master programme agreement
  5. Structured Exchange Agreement
  6. Exchange agreements

USI Faculty can find the description of the procedures to follow in order to enter into bilateral agreements: procedures for entering into and renewing MoU and academic agreements.

The bilateral agreement proposal form (to be completed in order to start the process) can be downloaded here.

The International Relations and Study Abroad Service is the main contact for the promoter of the agreement, provides templates and support in drafting and concluding agreements and maintains an archive of original documents.
If interested, please get in touch with the International Relations and Study Abroad Service by e-mail: relint@usi.ch.

A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) is a framework agreement that formalises the mutual interest of the parties in collaborating. It outlines the general objectives of the cooperation and the principles underpinning it, without regulating in detail how the collaboration will be implemented. As a rule, an MoU does not create binding operational or financial obligations for the parties and does not replace the agreements required to carry out specific activities. The actual implementation of the collaboration is normally governed by subsequent agreements/annex.

An agreement with a partner university that enables selected students to obtain both a USI degree and a degree from the partner institution. The study programme is jointly designed by the two universities and includes the mutual recognition of part of the academic work completed at each institution, while maintaining separate degree requirements and distinct final qualifications. Upon completion of the programme, students are awarded two separate diplomas.

Participation is typically optional and limited to a selected number of students who meet the eligibility criteria agreed upon by the partner institutions. Students who do not participate in the double degree track follow the regular study programme and are awarded only the degree of their home institution.

An agreement with one or more partner universities that enables students enrolled in a specific programme to obtain a single degree jointly awarded by the participating institutions. The programme is jointly designed and delivered by the partners on the basis of an integrated curriculum, which normally includes study periods at multiple institutions and the full recognition of academic work completed at each partner university.

Unlike a double degree programme, the joint degree is generally structured as a single, fully integrated course of study leading to the award of one joint qualification upon successful completion of all programme requirements.

Typically, one of the partner institutions assumes responsibility for the overall coordination and operational management of the programme, serving as the main point of reference for administrative, organisational, and quality assurance matters.

An agreement with a partner university designed to bridge academic pathways based on the 4+1 model with the Bologna 3+2 structure. Under this type of arrangement, students enrolled in a four-year bachelor's programme at the partner institution typically spend one semester at USI during their undergraduate studies, taking courses that form part of a designated USI master's programme.

After completing the mobility period, students return to their home institution to finish their bachelor's degree and obtain their undergraduate qualification. Upon graduation, they may apply for admission to the relevant USI master's programme covered by the agreement.

Thanks to the recognition of credits earned during their semester at USI, admitted students can complete the master's programme in three semesters instead of four, while fulfilling the same academic requirements as students following the standard study track.

A mobility agreement developed with academically distinguished partner universities and aimed at creating coordinated study pathways between the institutions involved. Unlike traditional exchange agreements (see below), students do not freely choose the courses to be taken at the host institution. Instead, the agreement defines a predefined package of courses that has been jointly designed and approved by the partner institutions.

The course package consists of modules that are either equivalent to courses offered within the home university's study programme or complementary to them, ensuring that the mobility period is fully integrated into the student's academic path. In addition to enabling the substitution of equivalent courses, these agreements may leverage the complementary strengths of the partner institutions by providing access to specialised knowledge, subject areas, or learning opportunities not available at the home institution. This may, for example, support the development of minors or other shared curricular pathways.

The objective of a structured exchange agreement is to ensure a high degree of academic integration between the participating programmes, while offering students a coherent and pedagogically meaningful international learning experience.

An agreement that enables USI students to undertake a study period at a partner university for one semester or, where applicable, for a full academic year, depending on the study programme. As part of the mobility period, students select the courses they wish to attend at the host institution and agree, prior to departure, on their academic recognition through a study plan approved by the relevant academic authorities. Upon completion of the mobility period, examinations passed and other academic activities successfully completed abroad are recognised by USI in accordance with the previously approved study plan.

Two main types of study mobility can be distinguished:

i. mobility within the framework of the Swiss-European Mobility Programme (SEMP);

ii. mobility based on bilateral agreements with non-European partner universities.

For mobility under point (i), the agreement framework and model are defined by the national agency. Mobility under point (ii) must instead be governed by a bilateral agreement between the participating institutions.

*In Switzerland, mobility between Swiss universities and the two Federal Institutes of Technology (ETH Zurich and EPFL) is regulated through a national framework agreement; therefore, no separate bilateral agreement is needed.
